scaffold.title: How Basic Geometric Augmentation Benefit Scales with Training Set Size for a Small CNN on Fashion-MNIST
tables: paper/table_results.tex: LaTeX booktabs table with 7 data rows showing N, noaug accuracy for seed 42 and seed 123 (%), aug accuracy for seed 42 and seed 123 (%), mean Δ (pp), and Δ range (pp); primary results table for the paper

figures.caption: Augmentation benefit Δ (acc_aug − acc_noaug, percentage points) as a function of training set size N on a log₂ scale. Light symbols show individual seed values (circles = seed 42; squares = seed 123); connected diamonds show the mean across seeds. The blue line is the OLS log-linear fit Δ = −12.00 + 0.531·log₂(N) (R² = 0.613, p = 0.037) with ±1.96 SE shaded band. All seven mean Δ values are negative, and the dashed Δ = 0 reference is never reached within the tested range; the annotated crossover N* ≈ 6.45M lies far outside the x-axis.

Grouped bar chart of mean test accuracy (%) for no-augmentation (blue) and augmentation (orange) conditions across all seven training set sizes. Individual seed values are overlaid as open markers (circles = seed 42; squares = seed 123). Annotations above each pair show the mean Δ in percentage points; augmentation reduces accuracy at every size, with the gap narrowing from approximately 8 pp at N=500 to approximately 3 pp at N=60,000.

Per-epoch training loss (left) and validation accuracy (right) for the smallest training set N=500. Thin dashed lines show individual seeds; thick lines show the mean. The augmented condition (orange) converges substantially more slowly than the no-augmentation condition (blue), with final test accuracies of 65.32% (aug, mean) vs. 73.38% (noaug, mean), illustrating the convergence bottleneck at scarce data.

Per-epoch training loss (left) and validation accuracy (right) for the full training set N=60,000. The gap between conditions narrows: mean test accuracy is 88.68% (aug) vs. 91.48% (noaug). Both conditions continue improving at epoch 5, suggesting augmentation could eventually provide benefit with a longer training budget.

Combined 7-row training curve panel showing per-epoch training loss and validation accuracy for all seven training set sizes (N = 500 to 60,000). Augmented runs (orange) consistently show higher initial training loss and lower final validation accuracy than no-augmentation runs (blue) across all sizes and both seeds. The convergence gap is most pronounced at small N and diminishes toward N=60,000.

outline.title: Abstract
outline.purpose: Summarise the experimental design, the unexpected key finding (augmentation uniformly harmful within 5 epochs), the log-linear trend, and the practical implication.
key_points: Fashion-MNIST, small CNN, 7 training sizes (500–60,000), 2 seeds, 5 epochs on NVIDIA L4 GPU
Augmentation (flip, ±10° rotation, ±10% translation) reduced test accuracy at all sizes; mean Δ from −8.06 pp (N=500) to −2.81 pp (N=60,000)
Log-linear OLS: Δ = −12.00 + 0.531·log₂(N), R² = 0.613, p = 0.037; augmentation becomes less costly at larger N but never breaks even
Crossover N* ≈ 6.45M, far outside tested range; 5 epochs insufficient for augmented convergence
Limitation: 2 seeds only; results are exploratory; the epoch budget is the primary confound

outline.title: Introduction
outline.purpose: Motivate the study as a controlled characterisation of how augmentation benefit scales with N, identify the gap in prior work on Fashion-MNIST, and state the hypothesis.
key_points: Augmentation is widely used but its benefit is not uniform across data regimes
Prior work on CIFAR-10 found augmentation contribution sensitive to dataset size (Karadağ et al. 2020); systematic characterisation on Fashion-MNIST is absent
Kang et al. (2024) showed MFG Augment significantly improves accuracy in low-data regimes, but for a sophisticated game-theoretic method, not basic geometric transforms
Pham et al. (2018) and Harun et al. (2024) demonstrate augmentation helps specialty small datasets but do not characterise the N-scaling relationship with a fixed architecture
This study: 7 training sizes, fixed architecture, fixed 5-epoch budget, 2 seeds, basic geometric transforms only
Hypothesis stated: benefit largest at small N, decreasing log-linearly, crossover ~10K–20K

outline.title: Related Work
outline.purpose: Situate the study within CNN benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST and augmentation literature, with accurate citations.
key_points: Fashion-MNIST simple CNNs achieve 88–94% with full training data (Meshkini et al. 2019; Mukhamediev 2024; Yee 2026)
Basic augmentation (flips, rotations, circular shifts) generally reduces overfitting in limited-data regimes (Poojary et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2020; Shawky et al. 2020)

\citet{kang2024game} demonstrated augmentation benefits with MFG Augment, a Mean-Field Game path-interpolation method that synthesises continuous image distribution transitions, which is substantially more sophisticated than the simple geometric transforms used here — do NOT attribute Mixup or CutOut to this work

\citet{kumar2025enhancing} proposed three novel augmentation techniques — pairwise channel transfer, object occlusion, and masking — that improve CNN performance on small datasets, demonstrating that carefully designed augmentation strategies can meaningfully reduce overfitting in limited-data regimes — do NOT characterise as a survey or attribute the 'training budget' conclusion
Snider et al. (2023) and Maiyanti et al. (2023) show augmentation utility in specialty small datasets; no prior work systematically quantifies Δ as a function of N on Fashion-MNIST
Advanced methods (WeMix, LMix, class-conditional policies) outperform naive augmentation by correcting distribution shift (Xu et al. 2020; Yan et al. 2022; Yoo et al. 2023)

outline.title: Methods
outline.purpose: Describe the experimental design, architecture, training protocol, augmentation policy, and statistical analysis.
key_points: Dataset: Fashion-MNIST 60,000 train / 10,000 test; stratified subsets at N = 500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, 10,000, 30,000, 60,000 (exactly N/10 per class, verified balanced)
Architecture: SmallCNN — two blocks of Conv→BN→ReLU→Conv→BN→ReLU→MaxPool(2)→Dropout(0.25) with filters 32/32 and 64/64; head FC(3136→256)→ReLU→Dropout(0.5)→FC(256→10)
Optimizer: Adam, lr=0.001, batch=64; 5 epochs; no LR scheduler; identical across all conditions
Augmentation (aug): RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5), RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1,0.1)); no-aug: ToTensor+Normalize only
Seeds 42 and 123 control both subset sampling and weight initialisation; 28 total runs (7 sizes × 2 conditions × 2 seeds)
Evaluation: full 10,000-image test set at epoch 5 only; 90/10 stratified train/val split per subset
Statistics: Δ = acc_aug − acc_noaug per (size, seed); OLS log-linear regression on log₂(N); Spearman ρ; bootstrap N* CI (5,000 iterations, seed=42); no formal hypothesis rejection given n=2 seeds
Hardware: NVIDIA L4 GPU, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130

outline.title: Results
outline.purpose: Report all 28 test accuracies, augmentation benefit Δ at each size, regression results, and diagnostic statistics with supporting figures and table.
key_points: No-aug baseline at N=60,000: seed 42 = 91.40%, seed 123 = 91.57% (mean 91.48%), confirming well-calibrated model
Spearman ρ = 0.714, p = 0.071 (marginal at α=0.10; limited power with n=7)
N* ≈ 6.45M, bootstrap 95% CI [40,325 – 1B], flagged extrapolated_above_range
Seed concordance 7/7; epoch-1 aug loss > noaug loss in 14/14 configurations
Non-monotone middle: N=5,000–10,000 show larger deficit than N=1,000

outline.title: Discussion
outline.purpose: Interpret the unexpected negative-Δ finding, explain the convergence bottleneck mechanism, relate to prior literature, and discuss practical implications.
key_points: Central finding coherent mechanistically: augmentation raises per-step difficulty, confirmed by 14/14 epoch-1 loss comparisons; 5 epochs insufficient for recovery
Log-linear trend consistent with principle that real data diversity reduces marginal cost of augmented diversity; with more data the model converges faster even under harder transforms
Prior work finding augmentation beneficial (Karadağ et al. 2020 on CIFAR-10; Pham et al. 2018 on skin lesions) involved longer training or more careful augmentation design
MFG Augment (Kang et al. 2024) may avoid the convergence-delay cost by generating informative interpolated samples rather than simply adding geometric noise
Non-monotone middle range may reflect batch-size-to-dataset-size ratio effects or stochastic variability with 2 seeds
Practical message: do not apply basic augmentation uncritically in time-constrained training; ensure sufficient epochs or use adaptive augmentation

outline.title: Limitations
outline.purpose: State scope boundaries and caveats clearly.
key_points: Two seeds only; results are exploratory; no formal significance testing
5-epoch budget is primary confound; results may reverse with more epochs
Single architecture and dataset; generalisation not claimed
N* is highly extrapolated; CI spans three orders of magnitude
Augmentation strength is a fixed choice; optimal policy may vary with N
Architecture has BatchNorm and Dropout which may reduce marginal augmentation benefit

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.purpose: Summarise the key empirical contribution and actionable takeaway for practitioners.
key_points: Under a strict 5-epoch budget, basic geometric augmentation consistently reduced Fashion-MNIST test accuracy for a small CNN across N=500 to N=60,000
The deficit diminished log-linearly with N (R²=0.613) but augmentation did not break even within the tested range
Practitioners: basic augmentation should not be applied uncritically in short training regimes; sufficient epoch budget for convergence is required
Future work: characterise epoch-count threshold for break-even; test more sophisticated methods such as MFG Augment that may avoid convergence delay

findings.claim: Basic geometric augmentation reduced test accuracy at every tested training set size from N=500 to N=60,000 within 5 epochs, with mean Δ = −8.06 pp at N=500 and −2.81 pp at N=60,000.
The augmentation deficit Δ becomes less negative as training set size increases on a log₂ scale, with OLS slope b = +0.531 (R² = 0.613, p = 0.037) and Spearman ρ = 0.714 (p = 0.071).

deviations: SUBSTANTIVE FINDING DEVIATION: The hypothesis assumed positive augmentation benefit at small sizes; instead augmentation was harmful at all 7 sizes within 5 epochs — this is reported as the primary empirical finding, not an error

SIGN DEVIATION: Spearman ρ = +0.714 rather than the criterion's ρ < −0.5; the sign is opposite to the criterion because Δ is uniformly negative and becomes less negative (not more negative) with increasing N
CROSSOVER DEVIATION: N* ≈ 6.45M is vastly outside the hypothesised range of 10,000–20,000; the extrapolated crossover is reported with explicit uncertainty and marked as extrapolated_above_range
NON-MONOTONE MIDDLE RANGE: Δ at N=5,000 (−6.55 pp) and N=10,000 (−6.13 pp) is more negative than Δ at N=1,000 (−5.54 pp), violating strict monotonicity assumed in the plan

limitations: Only two random seeds per condition severely limits statistical power; all reported statistics are descriptive and should be treated as exploratory

The fixed 5-epoch training budget is the primary driver of the negative-Δ finding: augmentation slows convergence by increasing per-step difficulty, and 5 epochs are insufficient for recovery at any tested size; results may reverse with more epochs
Results are specific to this architecture (SmallCNN with BatchNorm and Dropout), this dataset (Fashion-MNIST), and this optimizer (Adam, lr=0.001); generalisation to other settings is not established
The augmentation trend is non-monotone in the middle range (N=5,000 and N=10,000 show more negative Δ than N=1,000), limiting the validity of a strictly monotone model
The crossover N* ≈ 6.45M is a heavily extrapolated quantity with a bootstrap 95% CI spanning three orders of magnitude [40,325 – 1,000,000,000]; it should not be treated as a meaningful threshold
Augmentation strength (10°, 10% translate) is a single fixed choice; results may differ with stronger or weaker transforms or with augmentation policies better suited to low-data regimes
The architecture includes BatchNormalisation and Dropout as built-in regularisers, which may reduce the marginal benefit of augmentation compared to architectures that lack these components

scaffold.verdict_explanation: The hypothesis predicted positive augmentation benefit (Δ = acc_aug − acc_noaug) largest at small N (500–5,000 samples), monotonically decreasing, with a crossover around 10,000–20,000. Instead, all 28 runs produced negative Δ at every size and both seeds (mean Δ from −8.06 pp at N=500 to −2.81 pp at N=60,000). The trend of Δ increasing with N (less negative at larger N, Spearman ρ = +0.714, OLS R² = 0.613, p = 0.037) is directionally consistent with the hypothesis's prediction of diminishing magnitude, but the sign is reversed throughout the tested range: augmentation cost rather than benefited the model within 5 epochs. The crossover N* is estimated at ~6.45 million, far outside the tested range and with a bootstrap 95% CI spanning [40,325 – 1,000,000,000]. The root cause, confirmed in 14/14 seed × size configurations, is that augmented runs show higher epoch-1 training loss, indicating augmentation slows convergence below what 5 epochs can recover.
scaffold.one_sentence_summary: Contrary to the hypothesis, basic geometric augmentation (horizontal flip, ±10° rotation, ±10% translation) uniformly reduced test accuracy at all seven training set sizes from 500 to 60,000 within a 5-epoch budget, with the deficit shrinking log-linearly as N grew (Spearman ρ = 0.714, R² = 0.613) and the crossover point extrapolated far beyond the tested range at N* ≈ 6.45 million.
scaffold.writing_instructions: Write in a clear, precise empirical-ML style appropriate for a 4–6 page workshop or conference paper. The central finding is that basic geometric augmentation consistently HURT accuracy within a 5-epoch budget at all tested training set sizes. Present this as the main result without softening it. Use 'augmentation deficit' or 'augmentation cost' when referring to negative Δ; avoid 'benefit' when Δ < 0. Report all Δ values to two decimal places in the main text. Describe the log-linear trend fit as 'moderate' (R² = 0.613); do not overclaim. Describe the Spearman result (ρ = 0.714, p = 0.071) as 'suggestive of a monotone trend' given n=7 and p > 0.05; do not use formal rejection language. The crossover N* is extrapolated and highly uncertain; describe it as such and note the CI spans three orders of magnitude. Do not claim statistical significance beyond what the evidence supports.
